That reliance impairs inhibitory learning because safety cues (the voice, the timer) get credit for relief, which weakens the brain’s update that anxiety and its bodily sensations are survivable without a crutch (per Craske et al. 2014). On outcomes, meta-analyses of standalone mental health apps show only small short-term effects on anxiety with scarce or fading benefits at follow-up, and effects shrink when compared to active controls (Weisel 2019; Linardon 2019). What actually builds durable anxiety reduction are skills that increase tolerance to internal cues and uncertainty—e.g., interoceptive/situational exposures, willingness to experience sensations without a pacifier, and varied-context practice so learning generalizes (per Craske et al. 2014). Unless an app explicitly trains these mechanisms and fades safety aids, it’s giving you relief reps, not resilience reps—and relief doesn’t stick when the audio stops.

Lasting calm comes from riding a little without the supports until your brain updates that the wobble is survivable.
